ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Progress Note 3 — Sick Visit — Ada Lovelace

text.paragraph: No bowel movement for five days, with bloating and cramps. [S]

Mrs. Lovelace asked for a same-day visit. She had her first cycle of carboplatin, paclitaxel and pembrolizumab a week ago and took ondansetron twice a day for three days after it. She takes long-acting morphine 15 mg twice a day, with one or two 5 mg doses of the oral solution on some days, senna two tablets at night and polyethylene glycol once a day, though she missed some doses of the laxatives while she felt sick. She has not opened her bowels for five days. She feels bloated with cramping in the lower abdomen, but she is passing wind, has not vomited, and is eating a little. She has no fever. The vaginal bleeding has stopped since the radiation. Her pelvic pain is no worse. [S]

text.paragraph: Vital signs recorded on 2026-07-07; see the Vital Signs section. [S]

tr.td: Comfortable at rest; temperature 36.7 C, blood pressure 110/70, pulse 88
Mildly distended and soft, with active bowel sounds; mild tenderness in the left lower quadrant over palpable stool; no guarding, rebound, or tympanic distension
Alert and clear; pupils normal size; not sedated

Bleeding between periods and after intercourse, with heavier periods, a watery blood-stained discharge and a constant pelvic ache, for about five months; average pain 7 of 10 despite her opium tincture; a friable cervical mass found on examination and biopsied; cause not yet established at intake
S — Synthetic presenting problem anchored to her documented final illness; superseded by the diagnosis at the second visit.
Iron deficiency anemia from chronic blood loss: hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL, mean cell volume 74 fL, ferritin 5 ng/mL, with tiredness and breathlessness on stairs
S — Synthetic modern finding anchored to her documented final illness.

Adenocarcinoma of the endocervix, usual (HPV-associated) type, HPV 18 positive, FIGO 2018 stage IVB: a 5.2 cm tumor with left parametrial invasion, metastases to left pelvic and para-aortic lymph nodes, and bilateral lung metastases on MRI and PET-CT; PD-L1 combined positive score 5, mismatch repair proficient, HER2 1+; treated with palliative pelvic radiation for bleeding and carboplatin, paclitaxel and pembrolizumab, with specialist palliative care from diagnosis
S — Synthetic modern diagnosis made at the second visit, anchored to her documented uterine cancer; the cervical site is a synthetic choice.
Cancer-related pelvic pain, nociceptive and visceral, from the cervical tumor and its left parametrial extension
S — Synthetic modern diagnosis made at the second visit.

Long-term prescribed opioid therapy: opium tincture for recurrent pelvic and abdominal pain for about two years, measured at times with a household spoon, converted at intake to measured oral morphine; no opioid use disorder on a DSM-5 assessment; naloxone supplied
S — Synthetic modern history anchored to her documented laudanum and opium; not a claim about her real dosing.

Drug-induced constipation from long-acting morphine and ondansetron, a week after the first chemotherapy cycle: no bowel movement for five days, with bloating and cramping but passing wind, without vomiting; no bowel obstruction on examination; potassium and calcium normal; resolved with laxatives
S — Synthetic adverse drug effect; not a historical claim.

list.item:
Drug-induced constipation (K59.03). Constipation from long-acting morphine and ondansetron, made worse by missed laxatives, in the first week after chemotherapy. She is passing wind, not vomiting, and the abdomen is soft with active bowel sounds, so bowel obstruction is unlikely and imaging is not needed. Potassium 3.8 mmol/L and calcium 9.3 mg/dL are normal. Opioid-induced constipation does not improve with time, so the laxatives must be taken every day while she takes morphine. [S]
Polyethylene glycol 17 g twice a day and senna two tablets twice a day until the bowels open, then back to the usual doses every day.
If there is no bowel movement in 48 hours, call: a peripherally acting opioid antagonist will be considered.
Ondansetron only as needed after the first day of each future cycle.
Fluids and short walks.
Go to the emergency department for vomiting, severe pain, a swollen tight abdomen, or no wind.

Cancer-related pelvic pain (G89.3). No worse; morphine unchanged. [S]
Continue long-acting morphine 15 mg twice a day.

text.paragraph: Guideline basis: Use of Opioids for Adults With Pain From Cancer or Cancer Treatment: ASCO Guideline (Paice JA, et al. J Clin Oncol 2023;41:914-930) (2023)

Follow-up: Telephone check in two days. Six-week review next week. Next scheduled visit 2026-07-14: six-week review: bleeding and pain after palliative pelvic radiation, the first cycle of chemotherapy with pembrolizumab, blood counts, mood and opioid safety. [S]
